LeadRush 2 · bot behaviour field manual

LR2 Bot Lab

How a LeadRush 2 bot notices you, decides what to do, turns to you and pulls its shots. Every drill below runs the same rules and numbers as the game's bot code, so you can watch the mistakes a human makes appear for the same reasons.

01 · WATCH A BOT PLAY

Eight scenarios, one brain

The blue bot runs a compact copy of the game's brain: detection meter, the goal ladder every 0.25 s, reaction time, Fitts flicks with a minimum-jerk path, 125 ms lag on your velocity, bursts and recoil heat. You are orange, on a script. Nothing about the bot's choices is scripted.

t = 0.0 s

The tour plays all eight; pick one to replay it. In scenarios 2 to 8 the scripted player cannot drop below 10 health until its script ends, so the whole behaviour plays out. The duel is a real fight.

        03 · NOTICE

        The detection meter

        A bot never knows where you are just because you exist. While you are in its view cone and in line of sight, a meter fills at 0.9 + 9 / distance per second, faster if you move, much faster if you just fired. It must reach 100 % before the bot reacts. Out of sight it drains at 0.5 per second.

        04 · TURN

        Reaction, flick and where it lands

        After the meter fills the bot waits a human reaction time, longer when you are far off to the side. Then it flicks with one fast, bell-shaped movement whose duration follows Fitts's law, and lands near you, not on you: errors along the flick are about 2.3 times larger than across it, and calm bots tend to land a little short.

        05 · TRACK

        Tracking a counter-strafer

        The bot sees your sideways speed through a 125 ms lag, the same lag people show, and leads by 55 ms of that lagged speed. When you change direction it keeps swinging the old way for a moment, so its misses land behind you, right after each direction change.

        Hit rate, last 4 s
        -

        Orange line: your sideways position. Blue line: where the bot aims. Dots are shots: green hit, red miss. Misses cluster just after each direction change.

        06 · CONTROL

        Recoil and the pull-down

        Bots do not get recoil-free guns. Every shot kicks the view up, the bot starts pulling down 65 to 135 ms later, and how well it compensates depends on its skill and tires as the spray goes on. Late in a long spray a sideways weave appears. Four bots, same rifle, 24 rounds at a target 15 m away:

        07 · SURVIVE

        Armour and the ammo stations

        Every soldier, bot or player, has 100 health and 50 armour. Armour takes damage first and does not grow back; health does, after 4 s without damage. Breaking someone's armour makes a ceramic crack for both of you. Each map has two ammo stations that give back 120 rounds and 50 armour, then go dark for 20 s for everyone.

          Bots go to a station only when they are out of the fight: no target seen for 2.5 s, not under fire and nothing better to do than patrol, idle or follow. They pick the nearest ready station within 85 m and sprint if it is more than 6 m away. Scenario 6 shows it.

          08 · ADAPT

          Skill presets and the adaptive mode

          Four presets change the human limits, never the rules. The adaptive mode moves one skill value between them during the match, from how you play: your hit rate, how often you rush to close range, how often you crouch.

          PresetReactionAim speedFirst errorSettled errorHeadshotAggressionFlank chance

          Values interpolate linearly between the two ends shown, as in AdaptiveDifficultyTracker. Ends: reaction 0.52 to 0.76 s down to 0.16 to 0.26 s, view 95° to 132°, detection 0.80× to 1.38×, hearing 0.85× to 1.35×, aim speed 4.4 to 10.2.

          09 · WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM

          Human data behind the model

          LeadRush 2 uses these as calibration targets. The constants are hand-tuned to match the published behaviour; they are not fitted to a dataset inside this project.

          • Fitts (1954), J. Exp. Psychology 47(6)Movement time grows with log2(distance / target width + 1): the flick duration and why heads take longer to hit.
          • Meyer, Abrams, Kornblum, Wright and Smith (1988), Psychological Review 95(3)A fast primary movement plus corrective submovements: the flick, the 110 to 165 ms pause, then the correction.
          • Flash and Hogan (1985), J. Neuroscience 5(7)Minimum-jerk trajectories, s(u) = 10u³ − 15u⁴ + 6u⁵: the bell-shaped speed of every flick.
          • Harris and Wolpert (1998), Nature 394Signal-dependent noise: bigger, faster movements are noisier, so long flicks scatter more.
          • van Beers, Haggard and Wolpert (2004), J. Neurophysiology 91(2)Endpoint scatter is larger along the movement than across it: the 2.3 : 1 ellipse.
          • ESTA esports trajectory dataset and CSKnow (Counter-Strike player data)Real players' reaction times, crosshair placement and miss patterns used as targets: around 125 ms of visuomotor lag on a moving target, horizontal errors larger than vertical ones.
          • Aim-trainer studies (Aim Lab)Ranges of flick times and accuracy between new and expert players, used to space the four presets.
